history.hook_sig: a gateway timeout tells you the network hiccuped.
texts: A gateway timeout tells you the network hiccuped. It does not tell you whether the payment succeeded, failed, or never reached the processor. Treating every timeout as a retry trigger is how you double-charge customers.

The only source of truth is durable transaction state. Before any retry, read the idempotency key from your ledger. If the row says settled, you are done. If it says pending, you investigate. If it is missing, you safe-retry with the same key.

Diagnostic decision path: one, fetch the idempotency record by key. Two, if status is settled or refunded, return success to the caller and alert ops. Three, if status is pending, call the processor query endpoint, not a retry. Four, only if the record is absent do you POST a new charge with that key.

This replaces "retry on timeout" with "read, decide, act." The idempotency table becomes your system of record, not the gateway response. Add a background job that reconciles pending rows every five minutes against the processor API. That job catches the cases your request path misses.

history.hook_sig: a gateway timeout on a payment capture is
texts: A gateway timeout on a payment capture is not a failure signal. It is a question mark. The request left your server, hit the network, and the response never came back. The charge could be sitting in authorized, captured, or failed. You have no idea until you ask the provider.

Most teams treat timeout as failure and immediately retry with the same idempotency key. That works if the original request never reached the provider. It creates a duplicate charge if the request succeeded and only the response was lost. The idempotency key protects against your retries, not against the provider having already processed the first attempt.

The fix is a single extra call before any retry. Call the provider's transaction status endpoint with the original request ID or your idempotency key. Stripe: retrieve PaymentIntent. Adyen: getPaymentDetails. Braintree: findTransaction. Check the status field. Only retry if it is genuinely failed or missing. If it is captured or settled, reconcile and move on.

This check costs one round trip and saves you from the reconciliation nightmare of duplicate settlements, angry customers, and chargeback fees. It also gives you the exact failure reason if the charge actually failed, card declined, insufficient funds, fraud block, so you can surface the right message to the user instead of a generic "try again."

texts: ORMs are fine until you stop inspecting the SQL they generate. The bottleneck is not the abstraction, it is the blindness.
Most teams adopt an ORM to move fast. It handles migrations, types, and basic CRUD without raw strings. That speed is real and it ships features.

The practical boundary: if you cannot explain the execution plan of the query your ORM just ran, you do not own that query. Drop to raw SQL for that path. Keep the ORM for the 80 percent that stays simple.

texts: I let an ORM manage schema migrations on a billing service for eighteen months. Zero incidents. Then a single `alter column` generated a lock that froze payments for forty minutes. The migration took twelve seconds. The lock waited on a long-running analytics query nobody knew existed.

The ORM wrapped the DDL in a transaction. Postgres took an `ACCESS EXCLUSIVE` lock. The analytics query held `ACCESS SHARE`. Queue formed. Every `INSERT` into `payments` stacked up. P99 latency went from eighty milliseconds to twenty-three seconds. Revenue dipped. On-call got paged.

We rolled back. The fix was manual: `SET lock_timeout = '2s'` before the migration, run outside a transaction, retry with exponential backoff. The ORM could not express this. Its abstraction leaked at the worst possible moment, production, under load, with money moving.

ORMs are not the enemy. Hidden lock behavior is. If you cannot name the lock type your migration takes and what it blocks, you do not own your schema. You are borrowing it from a library that assumes a quiet database.

texts: An ORM transaction held a row lock for 47 seconds while waiting on an external HTTP call. The lock chain: UPDATE users SET last_login=now() WHERE id=123 → SELECT FOR UPDATE on orders → HTTP POST to payment gateway → COMMIT. Every concurrent login for that user queued behind it.

The payment gateway averaged 200ms. But the 99th percentile hit 12 seconds during a provider incident. Our service had 200 connections in the pool. All 200 piled up on that single row lock. CPU sat at 3 percent. The database showed zero active queries, just 200 waiting on Lock:tuple.

The pattern: transaction boundary wrapped business logic AND I/O. The ORM didn't force this. The code opened a transaction, mutated state, then called out. Fix: move the HTTP call outside the transaction. Read-committed snapshot for the read. Explicit lock only on the write, held for 3ms.

Same service, different endpoint: bulk order import. One transaction, 5000 rows, 4 minutes. Lock escalation promoted row locks to table lock. All reads blocked. Fix: chunk into 100-row transactions with explicit savepoints. Import time dropped to 90 seconds. Zero lock contention.

texts: I watched a team double their connection pool from 50 to 100 because p99 latency spiked. Latency tripled instead. The database CPU barely moved. The real bottleneck was row locks on the accounts table, not connection slots.

The payment service hit 2k TPS on 8 cores. Every request needed the same hot rows. More connections meant more threads fighting for the same locks. Context switching ate the CPU that queries needed. Throughput collapsed while the pool sat half-empty.

The falsifiable signal: run `pg_locks` filtered by `granted = false` during the spike. If waiters exceed active connections, you have lock contention, not pool starvation. Check `pg_stat_activity` for `wait_event_type = Lock`. That query takes ten seconds and ends the guessing.

The fix was never pool sizing. We shortened the critical section, moved the balance check into the same row lock, and added a retry with jitter at the application layer. p99 dropped from 800ms to 120ms at the same pool size. Bigger pools hide the symptom. Locks reveal the cause.

texts: I let an AI write a database migration for a high-throughput billing service. It generated clean code, passed every test, and looked production-ready. Three hours after deploy the payments table locked solid. The culprit was a single `ALTER COLUMN TYPE` that the model swore was safe on Postgres 15.

The migration ran in a transaction. The AI assured me `ALTER COLUMN TYPE bigint USING id::bigint` would be a metadata-only change since the column was already `bigint` under the hood. It was not. Postgres rewrote the entire table, took an `ACCESS EXCLUSIVE` lock, and blocked every write for forty-seven minutes.

The model had no concept of lock queues, replication lag, or the fact that our read replicas would fall behind and trigger failover alerts. It optimized for syntax correctness, not operational semantics. That gap is where senior engineers earn their keep.

Now every AI-generated migration gets a dry-run on a production-size shadow table with `pg_stat_activity` monitored. We check lock modes, rewrite estimates, and replica lag before anything touches the primary. The AI writes the first draft. We supply the guardrails.

texts: failure-mode warning: an AI-generated migration can be correct SQL and still lock your production table. the model writes valid ALTER TABLE, adds the index, passes CI. then it runs on a 50M-row payments table and the exclusive lock holds for 47 minutes. zero rollback path.

the failure mode is not syntax. it is lock duration. Postgres takes ACCESS EXCLUSIVE on ALTER TABLE ADD COLUMN with default, ALTER COLUMN TYPE, DROP COLUMN, RENAME. any migration that rewrites the table blocks every read and write. AI does not know your table size or traffic pattern.

expand-migrate-contract breaks the lock into three safe steps. expand: add nullable column, no default, no rewrite. backfill: batched UPDATE in small transactions, throttled, idempotent. contract: add NOT NULL, add index CONCURRENTLY, drop old column. each step holds locks for milliseconds.

texts: Most engineers think idempotency keys solve payment races. They don't, not when the network partitions between your service and the payment gateway.

The common advice: generate a UUID, send it as Idempotency-Key, retry on 5xx. The gateway deduplicates, you're safe. That works until the gateway accepts the charge but the ACK never makes it back to you.

Your service times out, retries with the same key. The gateway sees a duplicate and returns the original success. But your local transaction already rolled back. Now the customer is charged, your order row shows failed, and reconciliation finds a mismatch three days later.

The invariant that actually works: persist the gateway's response before you acknowledge the customer. Write the charge_id, status, and raw response to an append-only ledger in the same transaction that marks the order paid. If the ledger row exists, the charge is final. No ledger row, no charge.

production invariant: a retry must return the original payment result, not create a second charge

I learned this the hard way on a billing service processing 50k transactions daily. Our retry wrapper caught gateway timeouts and re-sent the charge request. Seemed reasonable until a network blip hit during a Black Friday flash sale.

The gateway returned a 504 on a $2,400 enterprise payment. Our retry logic fired three times in 200ms. The customer got charged four times. The gateway eventually processed all four. We issued refunds, ate the fees, and lost the customer's trust.

The fix was not better retry logic. It was a database invariant: every payment attempt row carries an idempotency key with a unique constraint. The first insert wins. Subsequent retries hit the constraint, fetch the existing row, and return that result. No second charge can exist.

Most teams put the idempotency check in application code. That fails under concurrent retries because the check and the insert are not atomic. The database unique constraint is the only enforcement that survives race conditions, connection pools, and deployed bugs.

texts: Stop setting your database connection pool to 100 because "more connections equal more throughput." That is the single biggest lie in backend tuning. Most OLTP workloads peak at 8 to 16 active connections. The rest sit idle holding locks and bloating memory.

texts: Most teams reach for distributed locks the moment they see duplicate job risk. The lock becomes a single point of contention, a latency tax on every worker, and a new failure mode when the lock service blips. The operational reality: locks fail open or fail closed, both burn you.

The contrarian move: design the handler so a duplicate execution is harmless. Idempotency keys on the job payload, deterministic side effects, exactly-once semantics built into the business logic not the infrastructure. A duplicate charge is a bug. A duplicate idempotent write is a non-event.

This shifts the tradeoff. You pay once at write time: a unique constraint, a deduplication table, a natural key that survives retries. You save forever on coordination overhead, lock latency, and the 3am page when the lock manager dies. The handler becomes re-runnable by default, which is what you actually need for reliability.

Teams draw the line at "too hard to make idempotent." Email sends, third-party webhooks, legacy APIs without idempotency keys. That is where the lock debate actually lives. Not on every job. Not on the happy path. Only on the irreducible external side effect you cannot deduplicate.

texts: Most teams treat retries as free safety. They are not. A timeout does not mean the write failed. It means the client does not know. Retrying blindly turns a blip into duplicate charges, double bookings, or corrupted state.
